title: Marketing an Apartment Community in Phoenix in 2027: What the Market Data Says
seoTitle: Phoenix Apartment Marketing in 2027: What the Data Says
seoDescription: Current public data on Phoenix apartment rents, concessions and new supply, where the sources disagree, and what it means for marketing and visibility heading into 2027.
excerpt: Phoenix rents are still slightly below last year and concessions remain among the deepest in the country, while new supply is slowing. That makes visibility and consistent pricing more important, not less.
imageAlt: Tall saguaro cactus with twisted arms among desert shrubs under a clear blue Arizona sky
imageIdea: Real daytime photo of a Phoenix area apartment community exterior with desert landscaping and mountains in the background, no signage or logos legible.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
The current public data says Phoenix is heading into 2027 with rents still slightly below a year ago, concessions that rank among the deepest in the country, and fewer new apartments being delivered than in recent years. For marketing, that means renters still have plenty of choice and are comparing deals, so the communities that are easiest to find and most consistent about pricing have an edge. The data is also less tidy than it looks, and the sources disagree on several numbers.

We are based in Phoenix, so this is our home market. Below is what the public data says as of early November 2026, with links, followed by what I would do with it. I am not forecasting 2027 rents. I have not found public 2027 projections I would rely on for a single community.

What is happening with Phoenix rents?

Rents are still down from a year ago, but the declines have narrowed. Apartment List's Phoenix rent report for October 2026 puts the city's median rent at $1,255, down 2.9% over the past 12 months, with a metro median of $1,347.

RealPage's third quarter 2026 update says Phoenix's annual rent cuts narrowed to less than 2%, and that Phoenix saw rent growth from July through September. Kidder Mathews' Phoenix multifamily report for the third quarter of 2026 describes lower rental rates than a year earlier and an average asking rent of $1,535 per unit.

Those numbers do not conflict as much as they appear to. Apartment List reports a median, Kidder Mathews an average asking rent, and RealPage tracks a change over time. They measure different things, so compare each source with itself over time rather than with the others.

How deep are concessions in Phoenix?

Deep. RealPage's July 2026 market concessions report says Phoenix topped the large market rankings for discount depth at 15.4%, even as it fell just outside the top 10 for the share of units offering concessions.

A month earlier, RealPage's June 2026 report listed Phoenix among the markets where more than 25% of units offered concessions, with an average discount of 15.1%. Nationally, Apartment List's concession rate data showed 31.3% of properties advertising a concession worth at least a month of rent in September 2026, using a different method.

So in Phoenix, a smaller share of communities may be offering deals than at the peak, but the deals being offered are large. We wrote more about reading competitor specials as information in concessions as a market signal.

Is new supply slowing down?

Yes, according to every source I could verify, though they report it differently. Kidder Mathews describes fewer construction deliveries and lower vacancy in the third quarter of 2026 than a year earlier.

Northmarq's second quarter 2026 Phoenix report says vacancy reached a three year low in the first half of 2026 as absorption ran ahead of new deliveries, and that deliveries were down 13% through the first six months. Nationally, RealPage's third quarter update says the gap between apartments completed and apartments absorbed was the narrowest since late 2015.

What I could not verify was a single, consistent count of units under construction or a vacancy rate that the major firms agree on. Their published figures differ by method, so I have left them out rather than pick one.

What do the main sources say, side by side?

None of these firms publish community level data for free, and your submarket can look very different from the metro. Use the metro data for context and your own comps for decisions. If you need submarket numbers, a paid data subscription or a weekly comp survey of the five to ten communities you actually compete with will tell you more than any metro headline.

What does this mean for marketing a Phoenix community?

When concessions are deep and renters have choices, the community that shows up first with a clear, consistent offer gets the tour. Visibility and accuracy matter more in this market, not less.

  • Win the unbranded searches. Renters comparing deals search by area and need, such as "pet friendly apartments in Chandler" or "apartments near the light rail." Make sure your Business Profile and website plainly describe your location, unit types and policies.
  • Keep the special identical everywhere. When the market is moving on price, a special that differs between your website, Google and listing sites costs you trust before the tour.
  • Read the market weekly. A quarterly report is too slow when competitors change specials every few weeks.
  • Lead with what does not need a discount. Location, reviews, management responsiveness and real unit photos help you hold rate when others compete on free weeks.
  • Plan for a slower pipeline. If deliveries keep falling as these reports describe, the advantage shifts toward communities with strong reviews and steady visibility already in place.

Questions we hear

What is the median rent in Phoenix right now?

Apartment List reported a Phoenix city median of $1,255 in October 2026, down 2.9% from a year earlier, and a metro median of $1,347.

Are Phoenix apartment concessions still high?

Yes. RealPage reported that Phoenix had the deepest average concession among large markets in July 2026, at 15.4%.

Is apartment construction in Phoenix slowing?

The sources we could verify say yes. Kidder Mathews reported fewer deliveries in the third quarter of 2026 than a year earlier, and Northmarq reported deliveries down 13% in the first half.

Why do Phoenix rent figures differ between sources?

They measure different things. Apartment List reports a median rent, Kidder Mathews an average asking rent, and RealPage changes over time, each with its own data and method.

Will Phoenix rents rise in 2027?

I do not know, and I have not found a public 2027 forecast I would rely on for a single community. RealPage did report rent growth in Phoenix from July through September 2026.

takeaways: Apartment List put the Phoenix city median rent at $1,255 in October 2026, down 2.9% from a year earlier.
RealPage reported Phoenix had the deepest average concession among large markets in July 2026, at 15.4%.
Kidder Mathews and Northmarq both describe fewer new deliveries and lower vacancy in Phoenix in 2026.
With deep concessions and plenty of choice, consistent specials and strong unbranded visibility matter more.
